title: What Stress Does to Your Body
hook: A jolt of stress is useful — it sharpens you for a real threat. The problem is when the alarm never switches off, and the body pays for staying on high alert.
key_points: Short-term stress triggers a useful 'fight-or-flight' response: faster heart, sharper focus.
Chronic stress keeps stress hormones elevated, which wears the body down over time.
It's linked to headaches, high blood pressure, sleep and digestive problems, and worsened anxiety or depression.
Managing stress — not eliminating it — is the realistic goal.
content_html: Stress gets a bad name, but the response itself is a feature, not a bug. The trouble starts when a system built for short bursts is left running around the clock.
extra_html: The National Institute of Mental Health distinguishes between acute stress — the brief, even helpful surge that sharpens focus and primes the body to respond to a challenge — and chronic stress, which lingers for weeks or months. During the stress response, hormones like cortisol and adrenaline raise heart rate, tense muscles, and divert energy to deal with the moment. When the threat passes, the body is meant to return to baseline. Under chronic stress it never fully does, and that sustained activation is linked to headaches, high blood pressure, trouble sleeping, digestive problems, and worsened anxiety and depression. NIMH's framing is realistic: the aim isn't a stress-free life, which doesn't exist, but learning to manage stress so the alarm can switch back off.

related.title: Building Everyday Resilience
related.hook: Resilience isn't a personality you're born with — it's a set of habits and connections you can build, the way you build a muscle.

related.title: Why Sleep Matters
related.hook: Sleep isn't downtime — it's when your brain consolidates memory and your body repairs itself. Skimp on it for long and the bill comes due in your health.

related.title: Understanding Blood Pressure
related.hook: High blood pressure is called the 'silent killer' for a reason — it usually has no symptoms, yet it quietly raises your risk of heart attack and stroke.

related.title: TIPP: Four Skills for When You're Too Distressed to Think
related.hook: When emotion is so intense you can't reason your way calm, a clinical psychologist's go-to is TIPP — four body-based moves that lower the intensity fast enough to think again.

flashcards.prompt: Why is short-term stress not necessarily a bad thing?
flashcards.back_html: The acute 'fight-or-flight' response sharpens focus and readies the body to meet a real challenge or threat. The harm comes from stress that's chronic and never resolves.

flashcards.prompt: Which is a documented effect of long-term, chronic stress?

choices.text: Raised blood pressure and disrupted sleep

flashcards.explanation_html: NIMH notes chronic stress contributes to problems like high blood pressure, headaches, sleep and digestive issues, and worsened anxiety or depression.
